en: Akolpok held firm.
When fired, musket balls could not pierce it;
When thrust ruthlessly, spears could not pierce it.
Unable to withstand your father's fury,
The Chinese fled in confusion.
“His coat is made of steel!”
Kongurbai, khan of the monks,
Marveled at that coat of your father's.
I, your luckless mother,
Worked its lining in silk,
Taking no rest by day,
Taking no sleep at night,
Biting at it tirelessly for seven years.
From staring at it,
My dear eyes grew weary;
From biting at it,
My dear teeth wore away.
When upon the khoja of Kokand
He inflicted humiliation,
When he laid down his commands,
When upon the khoja of Andijan
He wrought dreadful deeds,
Upon Alty-Shaar and Margilan
He inflicted humiliation.
Upon the lands that would not obey,
Your mighty father Manas fixed his gaze
And used his force.
Throughout the face of the earth, tumult
He stirred in those days;
From every land he reached, tribute
He took in those days.
Between Orenburg and Margilan,
I, your disgraced mother,
Had the intervening lands searched.
All the fine cloth from there to here
I had brought by force.
When did your mother ever sleep?
Not one day did she go outside.
To bring the fine cloth,
Your mother dispatched forty falcons of men.
I had white fine cloth brought;
Of filings from hard iron,
The finest, like sand, I had sifted.
Layering them eightyfold again and again,
I had them put into Akolpok.
Without shrinking, I sewed and toiled;
Without tiring of the sewing, working long,
Only in eight years did I finish it.
Then, when they plundered my possessions,
Accursed be widowhood!
When that coarse dog, roaring,
Broke into the palace,
That precious thing went as booty.
Most precious of all, my son,
When you enter, upon the golden throne,
The very throne your father occupied,
That fierce woman Akylai,
Having folded it five times beneath her hip,
Will be sitting upon it.
To Abyke and Köbösh's
Palace, go;
“Mother, grant me a gift,” say,
And bring Akolpok back from Akylai.
How fierce your mother is,
Learn that from this encounter.
Ask for it as a gift
And come wearing Akolpok.
I have further words to tell;
Again, orphan, obey me!
I will leave none of my words half-told;
Again, my son, understand.
Into Abyke and Köbösh's
Dreams your father the khan comes.
Folded at six places,
Syrnaiza, the spear your father took into jousts,
Is inside that palace.
Let me tell of Syrnaiza:
'A hand's breadth of it was ridged,
A hand's breadth of it was lacquered,
Covered in elephant hide.
Red gold and golden thread
Were wound around its grip.
When your father, the leopard Manas,
Leveled it in fury,
No enemy stood without fleeing.
Leveled at night, it flashed;
When a whip struck Syrnaiza,
It rang out like a kettledrum.
When thrust home and pressed hard,
It bent without breaking.
Your mighty beast's Syrnaiza
Satisfied the heart to behold;
Along its back, fine steel was set.
Putting all his skill to work,
The lame smith Bölökbai,
That meticulous craftsman, that dear lion,
Made it to perfection.
He covered it in leather,
Forged its metal from hard steel,
Poisoned its point and reddened it,
So that all whom it struck
Would worsen, their wounds not healing,
So that death would thus reach them,
So that they would be left helpless.
He fitted its joins well.
Six times he sharpened it,
Tempering it in human tears.
He stretched gold over its tassel.
Pleased with his every service,
A thousand mares from the herd
Were given to Bölökbai.
Syrnaiza, made by Bölökbai,
For that lion, your father Manas,
Was a treasure specially dedicated to him.
No person could find its like merely by wishing;
That is the keen weapon left by your father, Manas Khan.
From the palace of the six villains,
Ask for it as a gift and bring it back.
Do not begin speaking of other things,
My plump, gray-speckled white hawk,
My gray goshawk, my morning star.
Of all the things I have named,
Leave none, if you can help it.
If you can, to all six
Address well-reasoned words and return.
If they will not heed what you say,
If they will not give what is yours to take,
Quietly turn and come back;
Return without quarreling.”
Such is the story of the treasures;
Let me leave that here.
The great tulpar among living creatures,
Buurul—let me begin his tale:
“Crying in anguish to the one God,
Your father the khan who has passed away
Said, 'Let my collared little orphan ride him.'
That mighty courser among animals,
'Let my only child ride him after me,' he said.
Dedicating him to you alone,
He had an amulet fastened to his head,
Fearing someone's evil eye,
And had Bakai Khan rear him.
In his third year that Buurul
Turned his neck like a stag.
Learning that he was a courser,
Offering gold and treasure weighed in poods,
The khan of Bukhara asked for him.
He would not give him when asked.
Far from giving Buurul away,
'My only champion shall ride him,' he said;
No one without ritual ablution mounted him.
While your leopard father was alive,
He washed rice and fed it to him.
'My beloved son shall ride him,' he said,
And valued him as your very equal.
When he reached his fifth year,
He turned his neck like an argali.
If a ditch a rope's length wide lay ahead,
He crossed it without wavering and galloped on.
Knowing his excellence,
Offering gold and treasure from tribute,
The khan of Andijan asked for him.
He would not give him when asked.
Far from giving Buurul away,
No random person was allowed to ride him.
He had an amulet hung upon his neck,
'My destined only child shall ride him,' he said,
And had him reared at the treasury.
With a camel-bull's forelock and a short mane,
Short in foreleg, great in body,
A Karabair, a noble warhorse,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs,
A mighty courser born from the unseen—
Maiden Saikal's Algara
And this horse were siblings.
No sire claimed to have begotten him;
No mother claimed to have borne him.
He was truly a child of the unseen.
Buurul, a true tulpar,
Is the horse for you to ride home.
Ridden six months, he will not weaken;
Until his sixtieth mature year,
His teeth will not wear down with age.
Ridden seven months, he will not weaken;
Until his seventieth mature year,
His teeth will not wear down with age.
Ridden to the world's end, he will not weaken.
Your learning when you study lessons,
That Buurul, if you ride him home,
Will be your wings in this world.
Ridden on reconnaissance, he will not tire;
Ridden to war, he will not grow saddle-sore;
Ridden on a raid, my foal,
His back and head will not ache.
High-backed, with a low croup,
He will not suffer when ridden in the hills.
When he takes on his winter coat,
He is red roan, with a short mane;
When he takes on his spring coat,
He is dark roan, with an onager's back.
The courser dedicated to you—
Without catching and riding that mighty courser,
My foal, do not remain in this world.
When your noble father died,
The splendid horse among the herd in the foothills,
Thoroughbreds and coursers mixed together,
When Abyke, Köbösh, and the six villains
Raided and divided your countless horses,
When he saw that the villains Abyke and Köbösh
Were enemies,
Across embanked Suusamyr
That Buurul passed.
Leading sixty swift horses,
That Buurul fled away.
Not stopping at the sight of a musket,
Never grazing twice in one place,
That Buurul fled away.
Grieving for your father the khan,
That Buurul vanished into the unseen.
He had no tongue to speak with;
Grazing freely, roaming at will,
Buurul the horse keeps watch.
'When will the soul-mate chosen for me,
Semetey, arrive?' he wonders.
Counting months and reckoning days,
That Buurul keeps watch.
'When will Semetey arrive?'
That Buurul keeps counting.
Leading sixty swift horses,
My foal, when he first escaped,
He stopped upon a mountaintop.
He grazed upon nine hills.
From that day to this,
When has he stayed in any one place?
He must have explored the face of the earth,
Roaming over the world,
Grazing freely.
'When will the little orphan come?'
He must be thinking of you.
No eye can catch sight of him;
No one knows where he is.
Only the rocky mountains know his wanderings.
Choosing springs from which to drink,
Choosing grass to pluck in sheltered places,
Grazing on fescue-covered passes,
Stopping alongside the argali,
He must have explored the land tirelessly
And gone to unpeopled places.
On the side of Old Turpan,
On the near edge of Barbar,
In the hollow of the Lop forest,
Along the Lop River,
He must have spent seven years there,
Chasing with the onagers,
Playing to his heart's full content.
He must have crossed along Ak-Suu,
